dataset.what_one_row_represents: A single attempted orbital launch (1957–mid 2018), tagged success (O) or failure (F)
dataset.geographic_scope: Global — all countries that have attempted orbital launches

ana_01.label: Dataset profile — 5,726 launches across 62 years
ana_01.content: The launches dataset contains 5,726 attempted orbital launches from 1957 (Sputnik) through October 2018, with 5,384 successes (94.0%) and 342 failures (6.0%). They span 17 launching states, 366 distinct vehicle variants, and 40 distinct agencies. The companion agencies.csv has 75 organisation profiles. Note that 2018 is partial because the snapshot was taken mid-year by The Economist for its 18 October 2018 graphic-detail piece.

ana_02.label: Annual launch cadence (1957-2018) — 1967 was the all-time peak
ana_02.content: The world flew its busiest single year in 1967 with 139 total launches (118 success, 13 failure during the height of the Cold War — both Apollo programme tempo and Soviet reconnaissance flights). Annual cadence stayed above 100 most years from 1965 to 1989, then collapsed in the 1990s as the Soviet Union dissolved. Modern years sit around 80–90 launches per year, much closer to mid-1960s levels than to the Cold-War 1970s peak. The 2018 number (80) represents only the first ~10 months of the year.

ana_03.label: All-time successes by state — Russia/USSR 56%, US 29%
ana_03.content: Across the full 1957–2018 record, Russia (combining USSR and Russian Federation) accounts for 3,024 successful orbital launches — 56.2% of the world total. The United States is second with 1,585 (29.4%). China is third with 289 (5.4%), narrowly ahead of France/Europe-pre-ESA at 284 (5.3%). Japan, India, Israel, Iran, North Korea, the Cayman Islands (Sea Launch), and the United Kingdom round out the list. The top two states still account for 86% of every successful orbital flight in history.

data_table.description: Successful orbital launches by state, all-time

ana_04.label: Annual launches by major state, 1957-2018
ana_04.content: Tracking the six biggest launchers year-by-year reveals the structural arc of the space age. Through 1990, Russia/USSR dominates and the US runs second. After 1991, both decline. China starts at zero and climbs steadily through the 2000s. By 2014–2016, the three are roughly tied. In 2018 China takes the lead with 28 successful launches versus the United States' 27 and Russia's 9 — the first time China is the world's busiest launcher. Smaller programmes (France/Europe, Japan, India) sit in single digits but show steady growth.

data_table.description: Annual successful launches by major state, 1957-2018

ana_05.label: Soviet collapse — peak of 101 in 1982 to ~25 in late 1990s
ana_05.content: Russia/USSR's busiest year was 1982 with 101 successful orbital launches. Through the late 1980s the cadence held above 90 per year. After the USSR dissolved in 1991, Russian launches collapsed: the 1996–2000 average was just 25.2 launches per year, a 4.0× drop from peak. The fall is one of the most dramatic capacity declines in industrial history — and it took Russian launch cadence to its lowest level since the early 1960s.

ana_06.label: 2018 leaderboard — China overtakes the United States
ana_06.content: In the 2018 partial year, China leads with 28 successful orbital launches, the United States is second with 27, Russia is a distant third with 9, France/Europe at 6, Japan at 5, and India at 4. Total world successes through October 2018: 79. This is the first calendar year in space-age history in which China is the single largest launcher — the headline finding of The Economist's 18 October 2018 graphic-detail piece.

ana_07.label: Agency type — state vs private vs startup, year by year
ana_07.content: The dataset's `agency_type` column splits operators into three classes: 'state' (NASA, RVSN, USAF, CNSA, ESA programmes…), 'private' (commercial firms, dominated historically by Arianespace and ILS launching state hardware on commercial contracts, and SpaceX from 2008 on), and 'startup' (newer commercial entrants such as Rocket Lab, Sea Launch, Land Launch). Through 1979 every launch was state-flown. Private operators first appear in 1980 (one launch). By 2018 private + startup launches sum to 37 — about 47% of the year.

ana_08.label: Top 10 agencies all-time
ana_08.content: Aggregated to the agency level, the top operators by total successful launches are: 'US' (the generic US-state code, 1,089) and 'RU' (the Russian Federation post-1991 code, 597) at the head, then China's CN (289), the Soviet AE code (254), commercial provider ILS-Khrunichev (95), United Launch Alliance Atlas (71), generic Japan 'J' (69), SpaceX (64), McDonnell Douglas Space Systems (61), and ULA Boeing/Delta (60). SpaceX is the only post-2002 entrant in the top ten, illustrating just how unusual its rise has been.

ana_09.label: Failure rate falls from 54% in the 1950s to under 4% today
ana_09.content: Engineering maturity is visible in the failure-rate trend: 53.85% of all 1950s launches failed (28 of 52). The 1960s rate was 13.0%, the 1970s 5.1%, the 1980s 2.9% — the lowest decadal rate ever recorded, when Soyuz, Proton, and the Shuttle were running mature production lines. The 1990s and 2000s sit between 3% and 5%, and the 2010s rate is 3.7%. Reaching orbit went from a coin-flip-with-extra-loss to a routine industrial process in roughly forty years.

ana_10.label: SpaceX scales from 1 launch in 2008 to 17 in 2018
ana_10.content: SpaceX (`agency = SPX`, `agency_type = private`) appears in the dataset starting in 2008 (Falcon 1, Flight 4 — the first successful private orbital launch). Its annual cadence then climbs: 1, 1, 2, 0, 2, 3, 6, 6, 8, 18, 17 — for a 64-launch total through October 2018. By 2017 SpaceX alone was launching as much as the entire mid-2000s commercial industry combined. This trajectory is the single most-cited data point in The Economist's 'new contenders' framing.

ana_11.label: Cumulative successful launches — Russia still leads but China is closing
ana_11.content: Cumulatively across the entire 1957–2018 record, Russia/USSR has flown 3,024 successful orbital launches, the US 1,585, and China 289. Russia leapt ahead in the 1970s and never looked back in absolute terms. But the slope of China's curve in the 2010s is steeper than either of the other two — China added 167 launches in the 2010s alone, more than the US (187) and Russia (199) added in the same period.

ana_12.label: Decadal launches by major state — visible torch-passing
ana_12.content: Slicing launches by decade by state shows the handoff cleanly: 1960s — US 471, USSR 378 (US era). 1970s — USSR 866, US 259 (Soviet era begins). 1980s — USSR 931, US 153 (Soviet peak). 1990s — US 283, RU 411 (post-collapse decline). 2000s — US 214, RU 233 (parity). 2010s — US 187, RU 199, CN 167 (three-horse race). India and Japan grow steadily but stay an order of magnitude smaller.

data_table.description: Successful launches by decade and major state

ana_13.label: Soyuz-U is the most-flown launcher in history
ana_13.content: Looking at vehicle families (the `type` column) by total flights, the Soviet/Russian Soyuz-U is the most-flown orbital launcher in history at 632 flights. The Kosmos 11K65M is second (445), Voskhod 11A57 third (299), and Molniya 8K78M fourth (272). NASA's Space Shuttle ranks sixth at 135 flights. Eight of the top ten most-flown launchers are Russian. This entrenches just how much of the world's orbital activity over the last sixty years has been built around a small set of Soviet-engineered rockets.

ana_14.label: Private + startup share has climbed from 0% to ~50% of launches
ana_14.content: Bucketed into 5-year periods, the share of orbital launches flown by non-state operators (private + startup) shows a relentless climb. 0% through 1979. 0.5% in 1980-84. 5.1% in 1985-89. 21.0% in 1990-94. By 1995-99 the world is half commercial (43.5%). The 2015-18 window is 49.4% non-state — the highest non-state share ever recorded, with startups (Rocket Lab, Land Launch, Sea Launch) contributing 15.2% on their own.

caveats.content: 2018 data is partial — the snapshot was taken in October 2018 when The Economist published the article, so 2018 totals understate the full year.
We combine SU (USSR, 1957-1991) and RU (Russian Federation, 1991-) into 'RU/SU' to track a single political successor's launch programme — without this, the early/late series cannot be compared.

agency_type 'private' is a JSR/Economist categorisation. Some 'private' operators (e.g. ILS) launch state-built rockets on commercial contracts; others (e.g. SpaceX) are vertically integrated. Treat the trend as 'commercial share' rather than 'wholly new technology share'.
